query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn system was selected to reduce cost while retaining the mechanical performance of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi; prior work reported comparable or better mechanical properties after excluding Co. Research on FeNiCrMn has mainly addressed corrosion, while studies of related high- and medium-entropy alloys examined dynamic responses under tension or compression, different temperatures and strain rates, compositional changes, and the presence of cracks or voids. Those studies established that dynamic properties are sensitive to loading regime and material condition, but their different chemistries and defect states do not identify what governs FeNiCrMn. Under the constraints of retaining the Co-free composition and its strength–ductility balance, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains the dynamic behavior of solidified FeNiCrMn across temperature and strain-rate regimes? Define a controlled study capable of testing the hypothesis, its applicable boundaries, the prior findings that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In solidified Co‐free FeNiCrMn, the dynamic mechanical response is primarily governed by dislocation‐based slip avalanches whose activation and limited healing result in abrupt stress drops during high-rate deformation; these slip events become more pronounced at higher strain rates and lower temperatures, leading to increased yield strength and work‐hardening because the time available for dislocation recovery is reduced.
generation.material_initial_state: Solidified (as‐cast) Co‐free FeNiCrMn with a typical single-phase or dual-phase (FCC with minor BCC/SHEAR band precursors) microstructure.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to dynamic mechanical testing (uniaxial tension or compression) under controlled strain-rate and temperature variations.
generation.conditions: Temperature spanning from cryogenic to moderately elevated, and strain rates varying from quasi-static (e.g., 10^−3 s^−1) to high dynamic rates (e.g., >10^3 s^−1), ensuring the material remains in its as-cast microstructural state without extensive post-solidification annealing.
generation.structural_mediator: Localized dislocation density accumulation and emergent adiabatic shear bands or localized deformation zones that form as a result of slip avalanches.
generation.mechanism: A competition between dislocation nucleation and limited recovery (or healing) under dynamic loading conditions produces abrupt, avalanche-like slip events. At lower temperatures or higher strain rates, reduced thermal activation and time for recovery amplify these events, thereby enhancing yield strength and strain hardening.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under high strain rates and lower temperatures, stress-strain curves will exhibit sharper yield points with intermittent drops (indicative of slip avalanches), higher yield strength, and enhanced work-hardening; conversely, at low strain rates and/or higher temperatures, more uniform plastic flow is expected due to increased dislocation healing.
generation.baseline: Dynamic mechanical behavior under quasi-static strain rate at moderate temperature, showing smoother plastic flow with lower yield strength.
generation.boundary: Findings apply only to as-cast, Co-free FeNiCrMn maintained within its standard microstructural regime; results may differ if significant microstructural changes (such as grain refinement from severe plastic deformation or annealing) occur.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative changes in yield strength and the relative contributions of dislocation mechanisms versus other deformation modes (e.g., twinning) remain uncertain; the degree to which slip avalanche statistics scale with temperature and strain rate also warrants further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of as-cast Co-free FeNiCrMn samples and perform uniaxial compression or tension tests at multiple strain rates (from ~10^−3 s^−1 to >10^3 s^−1) and temperatures (from cryogenic levels to room temperature or moderately elevated). Use high-speed digital image correlation (DIC) and in-situ microscopy to track localized strain fields and detect discontinuous deformation events.
measurements: Stress-strain curves to determine yield strength and work-hardening rates.
High-speed imaging or DIC data to identify and quantify slip avalanches (e.g., occurrence, size distribution, and temporal spacing).
Temperature measurements to monitor adiabatic heating in localized zones.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, under high strain rate and low temperature conditions, the stress-strain response does not exhibit sharper yield points with intermittent stress drops (or if no significant change in the magnitude or frequency of slip avalanches is observed compared to quasi-static conditions), then the hypothesized mechanism of dislocation-mediated slip avalanches governing dynamic behavior is falsified.

The work-hardening behavior of the HEAs was systematically analyzed by adopting the modified Ludwik model. The Cr element improved the local deformation characteristics, and the coordinated deformation of the dual phase was carried out, improving the nonuniform strain and promoting the strength and ductility balance of the alloys.

The HEA exhibits exceptional properties, including a superior yield strength of approximately 1.8 GPa and a high hardness of around 454 Hv. These exceptional properties make it suitable for use in shock environments. Computational studies have reported an FCC–BCC phase transformation phenomenon in this HEA under tension loading, indicating that this phase transition can enhance ductility while retaining high strength []. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are new alloys that contain five or more elements in roughly-equal proportion. We present new experiments and theory on the deformation behavior of HEAs under slow stretching (straining), and observe differences, compared to conventional alloys with fewer elements. For a specific range of temperatures and strain-rates, HEAs deform in a jerky way, with sudden slips that make it difficult to precisely control the deformation. An analytic model explains these slips as avalanches of slipping weak spots and predicts the observed slip statistics, stress-strain curves, and their dependence on temperature, strain-rate, and material composition. The ratio of the weak spots’ healing rate to the strain-rate is the main tuning parameter, reminiscent of the Portevin-LeChatellier effect and time-temperature superposition in polymers. Our model predictions agree with the experimental results. The proposed widely-applicable deformation mechanism is useful for deformation control and alloy design.

Unlike conventional metallic alloys, which are comprised of a base (solvent) and alloying (solute) elements, high entropy alloys (HEAs) are a class of structural alloys first introduced by Cantor et al. and Yeh et al. that consist of multiple principal elements in equiatomic or near equiatomic concentrations. Owing to their multi-principal element compositions, HEAs are characterized by unique combinations of properties, including mechanical strength,,, hardness,, and wear, and corrosion resistance. The use of multiple principal elements in far-from dilute concentrations unlocks infinite possibilities of combinations of properties and functionalities that are not typically found in conventional metallic alloys. Numerous recent studies on 3d transition metal HEAs, such as CoCrFeMnNi,, CoCrFeNi,, CoFeMnNi, CoCrMnNi, and Co0.25Cr0.1Fe2Mn1.35Ni1.3, have explored the impact of temperature,, grain size, alloy composition, strain rate, strain levels, and phase transformations, on the mechanical behavior of these alloys. The equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi, or so-called Cantor, alloy is a face-centered cubic (FCC) single-phase alloy that has been regarded as a model system to many single-phase HEAs.
